summary: Orange reef fish with three white bands, native to the Indo-Pacific. Lives among sea anemones, whose stinging tentacles it is protected from by a mucus coat.
Tiny schooling fish from the Amazon basin with an iridescent blue stripe and a red rear half. One of the most popular community aquarium fish.
Close relative of the neon tetra from the Orinoco and Negro rivers. Easy to tell apart: its red stripe runs the full length of the body.
Native to Thailand's shallow, still waters. Breathes air at the surface using a labyrinth organ. Males are territorial and must be kept apart.
Hardy livebearer from northeastern South America. Males are small and brightly coloured; females are larger and plainer. Breeds readily in aquariums.
Fast, striped schooling fish from South Asia. Very hardy, and also one of the most widely used fish in scientific research.
Peaceful armoured catfish from South America that sifts the bottom for food. Best kept in groups over soft sand.
Tall, disc-shaped cichlid from the Amazon with long trailing fins. Calm in general but may eat very small tankmates such as neon tetras.
Round, colourful cichlid from the Amazon basin. Needs warm, soft, very clean water, so it is usually kept by experienced aquarists.
Large South American cichlid known for recognising its owners. Grows quickly and needs a big tank; it will eat any fish small enough to swallow.
Domesticated in China over a thousand years ago. Grows far larger than most people expect and does best in ponds or large tanks, not bowls.
Royal-blue Indo-Pacific reef fish with a black pattern and yellow tail. Has a sharp spine at the base of its tail, like all surgeonfish.
Small, vividly patterned reef fish from the western Pacific. Feeds almost only on tiny live crustaceans, which makes it hard to keep.
North America's most popular freshwater game fish. Its upper jaw extends past the eye, which separates it from smallmouth and spotted bass.
Common North American sunfish with a dark flap on the gill cover. Often the first fish people catch.
Native to Pacific drainages of North America and stocked worldwide. Has a pink band along its side. Sea-run fish are called steelhead.
Hatches in rivers, grows at sea, then returns to fresh water to spawn. Prized by fly anglers on both sides of the North Atlantic.
Long, ambush predator of cool northern waters with a duck-bill snout full of sharp teeth. Found across North America, Europe and Asia.
North American perch with large, reflective eyes that help it feed in low light. Prized both as a game fish and for eating.
Heavy-bodied fish with two pairs of barbels on its lip. A major sport fish in Europe; invasive in many other regions.
Hard-fighting predator of the Indo-West Pacific that moves between rivers, estuaries and the sea. Most start life male and later become female.
Coppery inshore fish of the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts with one or more black spots near the tail. Also called redfish.
Huge silver fish famous for leaping when hooked. Can gulp air at the surface, so it survives in low-oxygen water. Mostly caught and released.
Powerful Indo-Pacific reef predator and a top target for popper and fly anglers. Often called GT.
Fast-growing open-ocean fish with brilliant green, blue and gold colours that fade after it is caught. Also called dorado or dolphinfish.
Fast tuna of warm oceans worldwide, with long yellow fins in large adults. A major target for offshore anglers.
One of the largest bony fish in the ocean, with a long spear-like bill. A trophy species in big-game fishing.
